title: A string from a delay line
teaches: Physical models: Karplus and Strong’s plucked string, and struck bars and bells

blocks.text: **The sound.** Two plucks. The first is the usual synth pluck, built from the envelopes of lesson 3: a saw, with a filter envelope that snaps shut. The second sounds like a string, a guitar or a harp. It is not a recording. It is made from a burst of noise and one trick, and the whole trick fits in a few lines of code. You'll set it up at the end.

blocks.caption: A plucked line: a filtered saw, then a plucked string

blocks.text: The difference you can hear is in how the sound changes. In the saw pluck one filter closes on all the harmonics together. In a real string each harmonic dies away at its own pace, the high ones fastest, so the colour keeps shifting as it settles. The second sound does that because it is a simple model of a string, not a filter on a wave.

parts.title: The mystery of the noise that turns into a note

blocks.text: **The mystery.** In 1983, five years after Alex Strong first tried it, he and Kevin Karplus at Stanford published a way to make a plucked string so cheaply that even a computer too slow for almost anything else could play it.[^karplus] It starts with a burst of random noise, which has no pitch at all, and in a few hundredths of a second the noise turns into a clear, pitched note. What turns noise into a note?

A **delay line** does: a short memory that hands back each **sample**, one of the tens of thousands of numbers a second that make up digital sound, a fixed time after it went in. Make the delay one period of the note you want, a two-hundredth of a second for a note of 200 Hz, and feed what comes out back in. Whatever is in the line now comes round again every period, and anything that repeats every period is a tone at that pitch, however ragged its shape. Fill the line with noise, and that noise repeated is already a buzzy note.

Each pass of the sound through the line, one period long, is a **trip** round. Now add one small change on each trip: average each sample with the one before it. Averaging smooths out the sharpest wiggles, which are the highest harmonics, so each trip takes a little more off the top. The noise rounds off into a tone, and the tone gets darker and quieter as it goes.

blocks.caption: What is in the delay line, trip by trip, and the level of the sound below. Pluck to hear it.
blocks.task: Move to 40 trips round or more

blocks.text: This is a real string, simplified. A plucked string is a wave running to and fro between the two points that hold it, the bridge at one end and the nut at the other, so it comes back to the same place once a period. Every trip round it loses a little, and loses the high harmonics fastest. A delay line and a gentle filter do the same.[^model]

On a plucked-string engine, **Wave** is how hard the string is plucked. A hard pluck with a pick fills the line with bright noise; a soft pluck with a fingertip fills it with darker noise, and the note starts mellower. **Timbre** here is the damping, not the tone colour of lesson 1 in general: how much each trip takes off the top. Low damping rings bright like steel; high damping sounds like nylon, or a string muted with the palm. **Shape** is how long the string rings, by setting how much of its level each trip keeps.

blocks.caption: A plucked string. Make it ring for a long time.
The same string. Damp it, until it thuds.

blocks.text: Play low and high notes on the keys. Low notes ring for longer, as on a guitar, because the line is longer. Each trip loses about the same share, so a string dies after about the same number of trips at any pitch, and each trip of a low note takes longer. Nobody programmed that; it falls out of the model.

Karplus and Strong's string was an early success of **physical modelling**: making a sound by simulating the thing that makes it. A struck bar, like a marimba's, or a bell is modelled differently. It has a set of **modes**, ways it can vibrate, each with its own pitch, often not harmonics of the lowest, and each dying away at its own rate. A **modal** engine strikes a set of very sharp **resonant** filters, each one ringing on at its own pitch when struck, one per mode, with a short click. Change the spacing of the modes' pitches, and how long each rings, and you go from wood to glass to metal; a metal bar's modes are spread far apart and ring a long time, and wood's die quickly.

Blown instruments have been modelled too: a delay line for the tube and a model of the reed or lips at one end. Yamaha's VL1 of 1994 was the first commercial synth built on this idea. It could bend and growl like a real saxophone, and it was very hard to play well, because a player had to supply the breath. Today modelled strings, bars and bells are among the engines of many small synths, under three knobs like every other engine.[^modal]

Now make the plucked string from the opening. The synth here plays a plain saw with the classic oscillator, held like an organ note. Switch the Engine to the plucked string, then set how hard the string is plucked, how damped it is, and how long it rings.

blocks.caption: A plain saw. Make the plucked string.

blocks.text: The filter and the envelope still work as before, after the string. The string's own ring, set by Shape, and the envelope both shape the loudness, and the shorter of the two wins. At full sustain the envelope simply lets the string ring out by itself. With a short decay instead, it mutes the string early, like a player's palm.

blocks.caption: Four questions on physical models
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: Why does noise going round a delay line become a note?
choices: Anything that repeats once a period is a tone at that pitch
The delay line adds a sine
Noise has a pitch to start with
items.why: Repeating every period is what being a tone at that pitch means, whatever the shape.

items.ask: What does averaging each sample with the one before it do on every trip?
choices: Smooths away the highest harmonics first
items.why: So the sound darkens as it rings, as a real string does.

items.ask: On a plucked-string engine, what does more damping sound like?
choices: A duller string, like nylon or a palm-muted one
items.why: Damping takes more off the top on every trip.

items.ask: What does a modal engine model?
choices: A struck object's modes: several pitches, each dying away at its own rate
A delay line with no feedback
items.why: Bars and bells have modes that aren't harmonics of the lowest; a bank of sharp resonances models them.

summary: **Physical modelling makes a sound by simulating what makes it**, instead of shaping a wave.
**Karplus and Strong (1983)**: noise in a delay line one period long, fed back, becomes a note.
**Averaging on every trip takes the high harmonics first**, so the note darkens and fades as a string does.
**The engine’s knobs**: how hard it is plucked, how damped it is, and how long it rings.
**Low notes ring longer by themselves**, because each trip round a longer line takes longer.
**Modal engines strike a set of sharp resonances** to model bars, bells and glass.

model.title: What the model leaves out
model.text: A real string's loss depends on its material, the body of the instrument and the air, and the wave on it isn't quite one shape going round: a pluck near the bridge sounds brighter than one in the middle, because it starts the string in a different shape. Later versions of the model added these. Julius Smith at Stanford generalised the idea into digital waveguides, the basis of most physical modelling since.

modal.title: A synth that needs no samples
modal.text: A recording of a guitar note is one note, at one strength, ringing for one length of time. A model makes every note fresh, at any pitch, with any pluck, and costs a few lines of code instead of megabytes of recordings. That is why modelled strings and bells fit in small synths with little memory.

karplus.title: No multiplies
karplus.text: Strong came up with the algorithm in late 1978, and he and Karplus analysed it at Stanford. In the 1970s, multiplying two numbers on a cheap microprocessor took too long to do 20,000 times a second for live audio. Adding two numbers and dividing by two (a single bit-shift) was fast enough, so their string could run in real time on an 8-bit chip.
